lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on why rules beat strongmen
lead.head: Strong rules, not strong rulers

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 92

body: All of us start out, Ajay Shah said, as “lit­tle clue­less chil­dren” who want a strong man to run the state[[x1]], and ex­pect a Ram Rajya. “All of grow­ing up is about un­der­stand­ing how this ac­tu­ally doesn’t work well,” he said.
In this episode, Shah and Amit Varma took up what Shah called a great con­tri­bu­tion by “my clan of econ­o­mists” to po­lit­i­cal phi­los­o­phy: rules, not dis­cre­tion.
The economists’ claim cuts against in­tu­ition. “The state be­comes more ef­fec­tive, not less, when it shack­les its own hands with rules and takes away dis­cre­tion,” Shah said. {092-C01}
## Three ar­gu­ments

Shah built the case in three stages. The first is pub­lic choice the­ory[[x2]]: the strong­man is not a Ram but “a reg­u­lar guy”, with wants and needs, who makes mis­takes like ev­ery­body else. Living under his ab­so­lute power is “noth­ing less than a night­mare”.

The sec­ond comes from pub­lic ad­min­is­tra­tion. A strongman’s min­ions be­come lit­tle tyrants, so even an au­to­crat wants rules to bind them. Julius Caesar, Shah said, wrote laws for ev­ery­one be­neath him while stay­ing above them him­self.
The third is the economists’ own: the state gains power by giv­ing up dis­cre­tion. That of­fends the machismo of most civil ser­vants, Shah said, who like be­stow­ing favours on sup­pli­cants.
Varma added James Buchanan’s test: de­sign a sys­tem so strong that if the worst per­son imag­in­able is in charge, “they can’t do much dam­age”.
## Credibility as power
The episode turned on a 1977 paper by the Norwegian econ­o­mist Finn Kydland and the American econ­o­mist Edward Prescott, *Rules Rather than Discretion*. Both, Shah said, won the Nobel Prize for it.

Its les­son is that peo­ple watch the state and ad­just. Raise a promised low tax rate on global firms whose fac­to­ries are al­ready built, Shah said, and the move may be pop­u­lar, but every firm will price in the risk for years. “The state loses power by being op­por­tunis­tic.” {092-S03}
A cen­tral bank faces the same test. It must de­liver its in­fla­tion tar­get, Shah ar­gued, whether there is an elec­tion, a cri­sis or a drought.
“In the world of in­fla­tion tar­get­ing, there’s a beau­ti­ful slo­gan,” he said. “We say that say what you will do and then do what you just said.” {092-C07}
Hence what Shah called hand­cuffs as com­mit­ment de­vices: a state short of cred­i­bil­ity de­lib­er­ately makes break­ing its own rules un­pleas­ant for it­self. {092-C08}
## The road to growth

For the hosts, the stakes are India’s poverty. Growth, Shah said, comes from high-productivity firms that take years to build, and into which peo­ple com­mit “their money, their in­ten­sity, their pas­sion, their time, their chil­dren”.
Each ex­pro­pri­a­tion and each sud­den change of rules teaches them to hold back. “All these fears add up to a wet blan­ket,” he said. The re­sult is low GDP growth. {092-C12}
The same logic, Shah ar­gued, runs through con­tracts be­tween firms, crim­i­nal sen­tenc­ing, treaties and par­ent­ing.
Varma turned the idea on him­self. As a teenager he was “a rebel with­out re­straints”. Today, with rules for sleep, meals and ex­er­cise, he is “a rebel with rules”.
Shah summed it up: “Be quiet and pre­dictable in your life, so that you can be ex­plo­sive and cre­ative in your ideas.”
Varma had one ques­tion. “Have you ever con­sid­ered Twitter?”

second.label: Ancient Rome
second.head: Laws for all but Caesar
second.deck: Ajay Shah on the strongman who wrote rules for everyone beneath him

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Julius Caesar’s laws

body: Julius Caesar was no demo­crat, Ajay Shah said. He de­stroyed the Roman Republic[[x3]] just as Rome had started learn­ing how to dis­perse power. Yet Shah counts him among the great­est human be­ings and thinkers who ever lived. {092-S05}

Running the Roman Empire, Caesar did not want his min­ions choos­ing how to wield his co­er­cive power, each be­com­ing a local tyrant. So he started writ­ing laws and process man­u­als, so that all of them would act in ways he de­fined.

Shah called this rule by law: Caesar had ar­bi­trary power, but wanted ev­ery­one else to work in a pre­dictable, rules-based way. {092-C03} Amit Varma set it apart from rule of law, in which even the ruler is bound.

quote.text: Julius Caesar de­stroyed the re­pub­lic. I also hap­pen to con­sider him one of the great­est human be­ings who ever lived.

third.head: Drunk on a 1977 paper

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on rereading Kydland and Prescott

body: “Ajay Shah reads pa­pers the way other ado­les­cent boys watch porn,” Amit Varma told lis­ten­ers. One paper at nine at night be­comes forty by four in the morn­ing. {092-J04}
This time the paper was Finn Kydland and Edward Prescott’s, from 1977, which Shah first met in his first-year PhD course­work, when he was “a happy, giddy child”.
Preparing for this episode, Shah had an anx­i­ety at­tack[[x4]]: had he for­got­ten some­thing? So he went back and reread the paper that morn­ing, and was partly happy to find he knew it all.

But the reread­ing did more. “I also just got a lit­tle drunk with hap­pi­ness,” he said, “be­cause just the whole mem­ory, the feel­ing of being in first year PhD and dis­cov­er­ing these things for the first time came back to me.” {092-S02}

p2.title: Rules, not discretion
p2.deck: The case against the strongman, from Caesar’s minions to the parent who cannot bring himself to punish

quote.text: if the worst per­son you can imag­ine is in charge, they can’t do much dam­age.

box.title: Kydland and Prescott, 1977
box.text: Finn Kydland and Edward Prescott’s *Rules Rather than Discretion: The Inconsistency of Optimal Plans* came out of the ra­tio­nal ex­pec­ta­tions rev­o­lu­tion. It taught econ­o­mists to take cred­i­bil­ity and com­mit­ment se­ri­ously, and, Ajay Shah said, it won both au­thors the Nobel Prize. {092-R01}

sections.label: The strongman
sections.head: Wanted: a weak leader
sections.caption: the trouble with strongmen
body: Our pull to­wards strong lead­ers is old, Amit Varma said. Our in­stincts were shaped in pre­his­toric tribes of at most a hun­dred and fifty peo­ple, where top-down think­ing worked[[x13]]. {#tribes} The at­trac­tion to a strong­man “is baked into us and we have to fight it”.

Ajay Shah built his case in stages. Public choice the­ory says the strong­man is an or­di­nary per­son with flaws, so his ab­so­lute power is a night­mare; the rem­edy is checks and bal­ances, rule of law and dis­persed power. Public ad­min­is­tra­tion adds that even a strong­man needs rules, be­cause all his min­ions be­come tyrants in their own way.
## What weak means

Shah wants weak lead­ers[[x14]], and Varma clar­i­fied the word. It does not mean weak of char­ac­ter or in­tel­lect. It means lead­ers “whose abil­ity to act on their wishes is re­strained by a set of laws”.

Varma cited James Buchanan, one of the guid­ing lights of pub­lic choice the­ory: build a sys­tem so solid that the worst per­son imag­in­able, “whether it is Hitler or any­one”, can do lit­tle harm at the top. {092-C02}
Shah of­fered a test of his own. When some­one asks the strong­man for a wish, can he grant it? A good coun­try, he said, is one where the strong­man can do very lit­tle. {092-J11}
~ The economists’ ar­gu­ment, Shah warned, of­fends most civil ser­vants, whose machismo says: “I get to de­cide.”

quote.text: if the worst per­son you can imag­ine is in charge, they can’t do much dam­age.

portraits.caption: James M. Buchanan
portraits.credit: Atlas Network Official website, CC BY-SA 3.0

sections.label: Monetary policy
sections.head: Four per cent, no matter what
sections.caption: anchoring inflation at 4 per cent
body: In a good world, Ajay Shah said, a cen­tral bank prom­ises sta­ble in­fla­tion and de­liv­ers it, cut­ting rates when the econ­omy is in deep trou­ble and rais­ing them when it over­heats.[[x16]]

Firms whose minds are an­chored on 4 per cent in­fla­tion stop rais­ing prices at every dearer raw ma­te­rial or local wage rise. Bond mar­kets set­tle too. “If you have con­fi­dence about in­fla­tion for the next 25 years, then you have con­fi­dence on what in­ter­est rate you re­quire for a 25-year loan or a 25-year bond,” Shah said. {#bonds}
## A bleed­ing heart’s mis­take

In the 1970s oil shock, Shah said, American pol­i­cy­mak­ers saw peo­ple pay­ing more for petrol and un­em­ploy­ment ris­ing, and chose not to add to the mis­ery by rais­ing rates. A lit­tle in­fla­tion for some time, they thought. {092-S06}
Firms and bond mar­kets learnt that in­fla­tion was not guar­an­teed. Behaviour across the econ­omy changed, in ways harm­ful for growth.
India’s law now holds the RBI ac­count­able for 4 per cent[[x15]]. {#rbiact} But the regime is new and the RBI’s record “mid­dling”, Shah said, so an­chor­ing minds will take decades. {092-C05}
~ Amit Varma noted that Shah had pushed for in­fla­tion tar­get­ing from the 1990s, and that it took more than a decade and a half to be­come law.

quote.text: But the thing is, once you do this, you have un­hinged the ex­pec­ta­tions of the econ­omy.

sections.label: Focus on rules
sections.head: Manual labour
sections.caption: handcuffs as commitment devices
body: The prim­i­tive model of gov­er­nance, Ajay Shah said, is a per­son who looks at each sit­u­a­tion and de­cides. Finn Kydland and Edward Prescott move the real work into de­sign­ing the rule: if state X arises, do Y. {092-C06}
Officials then sim­ply live up to “a pub­licly stated man­ual”. The de­bates worth hav­ing are about rules, such as whether to tar­get the ex­change rate or in­fla­tion.

Rules may be com­plex. A bond could, by its own terms, pay no in­ter­est in a year when real GDP growth is neg­a­tive. What is not on is skip­ping a pay­ment after the fact. “You’re al­lowed to go com­plex­ity, but you’re not al­lowed to ex­pro­pri­ate peo­ple,” Shah said. {092-C10}
## The price of a bro­ken prom­ise

A state short of cred­i­bil­ity should wear hand­cuffs. Shah’s de­sign for a mon­e­tary pol­icy com­mit­tee[[x18]] gives the gov­er­nor, the chan­nel for po­lit­i­cal pres­sure, one vote among five, be­side four in­de­pen­dent econ­o­mists. {092-R03}

In New Zealand, he said, cen­tral bankers[[x17]] get a bonus for hit­ting the tar­get and lose money when they miss, all by press re­lease. {#newzealand} A missed tar­get can also mean a mea culpa let­ter set­ting out what went wrong.
~ Such de­vices work, Shah said, be­cause the lead­ers of such or­gan­i­sa­tions care most about the re­spect of their peers.

quote.text: So the work of doing pub­lic pol­icy is ac­tu­ally more meta. It is about imag­in­ing one rule at a time.

portraits.caption: Finn E. Kydland
portraits.credit: Narodowy Bank Polski from Poland, CC BY-SA 2.0

sections.label: Growth
sections.head: Where great firms come from
sections.caption: rules as the machinery of growth
body: India is still poor, Amit Varma said, with hun­dreds of mil­lions of peo­ple in poverty, and growth is the way out. What do rules have to do with it?

They are of first-order im­por­tance, Ajay Shah an­swered. Growth comes from high-productivity firms[[x19]] con­trol­ling large amounts of labour and cap­i­tal, and such firms come out of the “toil, sweat, and tears” of peo­ple who spend years build­ing them.
This is not a quick startup chas­ing an exit at 10X, he said, but the hard work of build­ing large, com­plex or­gan­i­sa­tions.
## The pri­vate sec­tor is watch­ing

Whether any­one makes that ef­fort de­pends on the state. The pri­vate sec­tor, Shah said, is not stupid: it watches pat­terns. Expropriate one per­son today, and oth­ers fear they will be next. Create a mo­nop­oly PSU in one busi­ness, and oth­ers fear one in theirs.

Foreign firms worry that a na­tional cham­pion will get the gov­ern­ment to rig the game. The fears add up, Shah said: peo­ple hold glob­ally di­ver­si­fied as­sets, wait and see, and GDP growth stays low. {092-C12}
~ India needs this more than rich coun­tries, Shah ar­gued, given its in­sti­tu­tional mis­trust: of­fi­cials should face daily press con­fer­ences and un­scripted town halls. {092-C11}

quote.text: Firms don’t come out of thin air.

sections.label: Amit’s thoughts
sections.head: Orders, and when to break them
sections.caption: rules that leave room to adapt
body: Amit Varma raised doubts. Rules can be rigid: India, he said, cit­ing an ear­lier dis­cus­sion of Shah’s, has one Maggi and one Kit Kat, while Japan has thirty va­ri­eties of Kit Kat[[x21]]. {092-J14}

He re­called General Sagat Singh[[x20]], who at Nathu La and Cho La dis­obeyed an order from high com­mand be­cause he un­der­stood local con­di­tions, which later helped India enor­mously. Varma’s ten­ta­tive fix: build com­plex­ity into the rules, so they say when dis­cre­tion ap­plies. {092-S08}
Ajay Shah agreed. Great mil­i­taries split strat­egy, op­er­a­tions and tac­tics, each level own­ing its own sphere. In gov­ern­ment, the an­swer is de­cen­tral­i­sa­tion.
## Kodak’s strait­jacket

Rules can also sti­fle firms, Varma said. Citing Clayton Christensen’s *The Innovator’s Dilemma*, he noted that Kodak had the know-how for dig­i­tal pho­tog­ra­phy but could not make the move. Google, in the early 2000s, let staff spend time on pas­sion projects. {092-S09}

Shah agreed about firms. But a city like Liverpool, he said, has wanted the same ba­sics for hun­dreds of years: streets, parks, solid waste man­age­ment, water and san­i­ta­tion. The ex­cep­tion is mil­i­tary af­fairs, where Russia’s in­va­sion of Ukraine has set off an in­no­va­tion spi­ral.
~ Could lost trust be re­built? Policy lasts, Shah said, only when an in­tel­lec­tual com­mu­nity guards it, not when econ­o­mists “whis­per in the ears of Aurangzeb”. {092-J05}

quote.text: You have to fol­low or­ders, oth­er­wise a whole ed­i­fice can col­lapse. But at the same time you also need that local dis­cre­tion.

portraits.caption: Clayton Christensen
portraits.credit: World Economic Forum from Cologny, Switzerland, CC BY-SA 2.0

sections.label: Beyond economics
sections.head: Bullies, judges and parents
sections.caption: contracts, courts, treaties and children
body: The frame­work reaches far be­yond eco­nom­ics, Ajay Shah said, start­ing with con­tracts be­tween firms.

Many large Indian firms buy­ing a hum­ble part be­lieve a hun­dred sup­pli­ers are des­per­ate to sell to them. {#vendors} So they drive hard bar­gains, ex­tract work­ing-capital credit from small firms[[x22]] and prac­tise gunda­giri, break­ing con­tracts when it suits them.

Small firms build that into their ex­pec­ta­tions and shade their bids up­ward, so the bully pays more than firms that be­have well. Opportunism may win one pro­cure­ment, Shah said. “But like what about the fu­ture?” {092-S10}
## Courts, treaties and homes

In crim­i­nal law he favours sen­tenc­ing guide­lines, be­cause wide dis­cre­tion opens a Pandora’s box of doubts about fair play and tempts crim­i­nals to bet on le­niency. A strong­man who walks out of a treaty is cheered at home, but every part­ner learns his coun­try can­not be trusted. {092-C15}

Then par­ent­ing. No par­ent wants to pun­ish a child, Shah said, so when the mo­ment comes it is tempt­ing to let it go. That is how a par­ent loses cred­i­bil­ity, and chil­dren raised on moods learn to game the par­ent. {092-S11}
~ What works, he said, is pre­dictable rules that evolve grad­u­ally, not mi­cro­man­age­ment, and not a yes today and a no to­mor­row.

quote.text: And yet, when you do that, ac­tu­ally you’ve lost all your cred­i­bil­ity, you’ve lost your com­mit­ment.

It is wise and ef­fi­cient for the state to shed dis­cre­tion, to shed power, to lose power, to cre­ate a se­ries of pro­vi­sions and mech­a­nisms through which vi­o­lat­ing the rule will be­come un­pleas­ant for the state.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: A tax grab, a poker table, a finance minister and a reformed rebel

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s thought experiment on a tax raid that backfires
stories.head: The hostages have long memories
body: Ireland, Ajay Shah said, set a very low cor­po­rate tax rate. Global com­pa­nies chose to put fac­to­ries and of­fices there, and it pow­ered great Irish growth. He would rec­om­mend the same for India: very low cor­po­rate tax, ide­ally zero.
Then he imag­ined a bad turn: an eco­nomic down­turn, or a great earth­quake, with the peo­ple suf­fer­ing. A pol­i­cy­maker says the 5 per cent rate must rise, just for two or three years.

Shah called him “the clever pol­icy maker, it’s Indian IAS level of IQ”. {092-J03} The fac­to­ries are al­ready built, so the firms are hostages[[x23]]. They can’t leave. Why not grab a lit­tle of their money?
The move is pop­u­lar. The press praises it. It might even win an elec­tion. Until the 1970s, Shah said, this kind of rea­son­ing was nor­mal among econ­o­mists.

But firms in­vest on five-, 10- and 25-year hori­zons. A firm that built its fac­tory ex­pect­ing an 8 per cent re­turn on eq­uity in dol­lars now finds it is 6 per cent, and its cal­cu­la­tions are up­ended. {#roe}

Worse, it now as­sumes it can be socked again. Every fu­ture spread­sheet car­ries a higher tax rate as a safety fac­tor, or a higher re­quired re­turn to pay for the risk, and for years the low tax rate loses its pull. {092-S03}
~ People have long mem­o­ries, Shah said. They re­mem­ber the pe­riod when the state “stole so much money from the com­pa­nies”, and won­der whether it will do it again.
stories.why: Opportunism looks like a free win, but it spends the cred­i­bil­ity that made the pol­icy work in the first place. People are not fools, Shah said: they look ahead, watch the pol­i­cy­maker and ad­just. {092-C04}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the Irish tax grab

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a lesson from the poker table
stories.head: The four-bet that meant nothing
body: Most poker, Amit Varma said, is ex­ploita­tive[[x24]]. You spot a mis­take the table keeps mak­ing, such as fold­ing too much, and ad­just to profit from it.
The trap is as­sum­ing the table will not ad­just back. That, he said, is “why ex­ploita­tive poker is also au­to­mat­i­cally ex­ploitable poker”. {092-S04}

In the 2000s, Varma read a canon­i­cal poker book which said a four-bet, a re-raise of a re-raise, is al­most al­ways aces. By the time he was a pro­fes­sional, it was often noth­ing at all. “Everybody read the book,” Ajay Shah said, “and said, Oh, I can ex­ploit this.”
~ Varma took the les­son to taxes. In the 1970s, he said, Indira Gandhi had a top tax rate of, he thought, 97 per cent[[x25]], and India was not a boom­ing econ­omy. {#ninetyseven}
stories.why: People re­spond to your ac­tions, Varma said, so the world does not stand still while you ex­ploit it. Raise a tax rate too far and col­lec­tions can ac­tu­ally fall, be­cause peo­ple change their be­hav­iour.

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on how India’s growth episode went bust
stories.head: Taxed today for yesterday
body: It takes decades to build trust and an in­stant to lose it, Amit Varma said, and India’s growth episode from 1991 to 2011 showed how. {092-S07}

After the ter­ror at­tacks in Bombay, Manmohan Singh moved his most ca­pa­ble man, P. Chidambaram[[x26]], from fi­nance to the home min­istry. Sonia Gandhi gave fi­nance to Pranab Mukherjee, and Singh, who had health is­sues, did not take it him­self.

Varma called Mukherjee a “wild evil courtier” with no knowl­edge of eco­nom­ics, who came up with one dis­as­trous mea­sure after an­other. The worst was ret­ro­spec­tive tax­a­tion[[x27]]: telling com­pa­nies that new tax rules ap­plied to the past too, so they owed dues. {#retro}
~ It de­stroys trust, he said, es­pe­cially among for­eign in­vestors, whom India needs. In those twenty years, dif­fer­ent par­ties had gov­erned with the nation’s in­ter­ests at heart. {#parties}
stories.why: Retrospective tax is the ul­ti­mate dis­cre­tionary am­bush, and Varma feared India would take years, if not decades, to re­cover from it. Bad pol­icy is bad pol­icy, he said, which­ever po­lit­i­cal party is in power.

stories.kicker: Amit Varma turns the episode’s idea on himself
stories.head: The rebel goes to bed early
body: At fif­teen, six­teen and sev­en­teen, Amit Varma said, he was a rebel with­out a cause, “or if we wish to al­lit­er­ate, a rebel with­out re­straints”. {092-J01}
He stayed up late, worked three days in a row, drank beer with friends when he felt like it, skipped ex­er­cise and ate any­thing. All of it, he now thinks, worked against re­bel­lion. {092-S01}

Today he tries to sleep at least eight hours, eat at pre­dictable times and watch his diet, es­pe­cially after a re­cent health episode[[x28]]. {#sleep} On ex­er­cise, he ad­mits, it is “do as I say, don’t do as I do”.

~ The rules are a scaf­fold­ing to take off from, he said, like the al­go­rithms that let Elon Musk’s rocket be caught on its re­turn. Just as a con­sti­tu­tion con­strains the state, not the peo­ple, his rules con­strain his bad habits.

quote.text: Those rules aren’t con­straints. They help us be­come the best ver­sion of our­selves.

stories.postscript: Ajay Shah’s bi­ceps, Varma pointed out on cam­era, came from a rules-based regime, not from what­ever ex­er­cise he felt like. {092-J07}

quiz.q: In Ajay Shah’s three-stage case against the strongman, what is the economists’ own argument?
quiz.a: That the state be­comes more ef­fec­tive, not less, when it shack­les its own hands.

quiz.q: What separates rule by law, as practised by Julius Caesar, from rule of law?
quiz.a: Rule by law binds ev­ery­one ex­cept the ruler; rule of law binds the ruler too.

quiz.q: Which line from Shakespeare’s *Julius Caesar* did Ajay Shah turn into his economics slogan?
quiz.a: “You are not wood, you are not stones, but men”, adding “you will op­ti­mize”.

quiz.q: In Shah’s design for a monetary policy committee, how many of five votes face political pressure?
quiz.a: Just one, the governor’s; the other four be­long to in­de­pen­dent pri­vate econ­o­mists.

quiz.q: According to a canonical poker book Amit Varma read in the 2000s, what did a four-bet mean?
quiz.a: Almost al­ways aces, though by his pro­fes­sional days it often meant noth­ing at all.

quiz.q: Which single exercise does Ajay Shah recommend for anyone too lazy to do more?
quiz.a: Rowing on a ma­chine, car­dio that uses about 80 to 85 per cent of mus­cles.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 92. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: James M. Buchanan (Atlas Network Official website, CC BY-SA 3.0); Finn E. Kydland (Narodowy Bank Polski from Poland, CC BY-SA 2.0); Clayton Christensen (World Economic Forum from Cologny, Switzerland, CC BY-SA 2.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: Rules Rather than Discretion: The Inconsistency of Optimal Plans
shelf.creator: Finn E. Kydland and Edward C. Prescott
shelf.why: It is a land­mark of the ra­tio­nal ex­pec­ta­tions rev­o­lu­tion and, Ajay notes, part of the work be­hind both authors’ Nobel Prizes.

shelf.title: The Equity Premium: A Puzzle
shelf.creator: Rajnish Mehra and Edward Prescott
shelf.why: Ajay calls it an ‘amaz­ing paper’, co-written by a friend of the show with one of the au­thors of the episode’s key paper.

shelf.title: Designing the Monetary Policy Committee
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s de­sign for a mon­e­tary pol­icy com­mit­tee as a com­mit­ment de­vice: the gov­ern­ment-appointed gov­er­nor sits with four in­de­pen­dent econ­o­mists, so only one of five votes is ex­posed to po­lit­i­cal pres­sure.

shelf.title: The policy posture as an incomplete contract
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay ex­plains why no law truly pre-commits the state, since any law can be amended to­mor­row: re­forms stick only when an in­tel­lec­tual com­mu­nity, a cred­i­ble team and hon­est com­mu­ni­ca­tion stand be­hind them.

shelf.title: Why the RBI communication to government on the failure to meet inflation target must be placed in the public domain
shelf.creator: The Indian Express
shelf.why: It makes the case for pub­lish­ing the RBI’s ex­pla­na­tion for miss­ing its tar­get.

shelf.title: The Calculus of Consent
shelf.creator: Gordon Tullock & James Buchanan
shelf.why: The found­ing text of pub­lic choice the­ory, which frames a con­sti­tu­tion as the ‘rules of the game’ that should ide­ally rest on con­sen­sus.

shelf.title: A rowing machine (the Concept2 is the most common)
shelf.creator: Concept2
shelf.why: If you are lazy and will com­mit to only one ex­er­cise, make it row­ing.

shelf.title: Beware of These Five Fallacies! (Episode 45)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: How in­stincts evolved in small hunter-gatherer tribes mis­lead us in large, com­plex so­ci­eties: zero-sum think­ing, top-down think­ing, blind­ness to spon­ta­neous order and the pull of strong lead­ers.

shelf.title: Poker and Life (Episode 38)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: What Amit’s five years as a pro­fes­sional poker player taught him about life: most of what hap­pens is luck, so don’t let suc­cess go to your head or fail­ure crush you, and focus on doing the right things.

shelf.title: Inflation Targeting Rocks! (Episode 68)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The full story of in­fla­tion tar­get­ing, which Ajay pushed for from the 1990s and which took more than fif­teen years to be­come law: a les­son in how slowly good pol­icy ar­rives.

shelf.title: Don’t Mess With the Exchange Rate (Episode 67)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why the ex­change rate is the most im­por­tant price in the econ­omy and should be set by the mar­ket: rig­ging it to make ex­porters look com­pet­i­tive is a trans­fer from the poor, and man­ag­ing it in­vites cur­rency crises.

shelf.title: The Vintage Book of Indian Writing 1947–1997
shelf.creator: Edited by Salman Rushdie & Elizabeth West
shelf.why: An an­thol­ogy that opens with Nehru’s ‘Tryst with Destiny’, which Ajay calls one of the tran­scen­den­tal pieces of Indian writ­ing and ev­i­dence that great lead­ers can con­vey com­plex ideas.

shelf.title: How to Do Development (Episode 57)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The case, built on Lant Pritchett’s ev­i­dence, that every human wel­fare in­di­ca­tor tracks per capita GDP, so sus­tained growth, not re­dis­tri­bu­tion or small solv­able projects, is the way out of poverty.

shelf.title: From Imperial to Adaptive Firms (Episode 37)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: How Indian firms moved from re­gional satraps in the 1980s to top-down ‘imperial’ firms with uni­form best prac­tices, and then to ‘adaptive’ firms that pair rules with local flex­i­bil­ity.

shelf.title: Probal DasGupta Goes to the Himalayas With Books in His Bag (Episode 412 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit dis­cussed in de­tail with the mil­i­tary his­to­rian the ten­sion be­tween obey­ing or­ders and using local dis­cre­tion.

shelf.title: The Age of Hybrid Warfare (Episode 84)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why, in mod­ern con­flict, you may not know whether you have been at­tacked or by whom, and why covert, op­por­tunis­tic at­tacks such as crip­pling an­other country’s pay­roll sys­tem are the strat­egy of rogue na­tions and back­fire in the long run.

shelf.title: The Innovator’s Dilemma
shelf.creator: Clayton Christensen
shelf.why: Why dom­i­nant com­pa­nies like Kodak can have the know-how to adapt yet fail, trapped by their own pro­cesses, pri­or­i­ties and in­cen­tives, while dis­rup­tion comes from small up­starts.

shelf.title: The Heart of Disruption (Episode 86)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why big com­pa­nies crum­ble when they can’t adapt and how some es­cape that fate, told through Netflix’s 2007 stream­ing bet and the first half of Amit’s own startup saga.

shelf.title: Understanding India’s Pensions Disaster (Episode 65)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A first-principles ac­count of pen­sion re­form: how a small com­mu­nity with a shared phi­los­o­phy built the NPS, and how guar­an­tees and the old mess re­turned once that com­mu­nity dis­persed and its knowl­edge faded.

shelf.title: The journey of Indian finance (Episode 71)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: An insider’s ac­count of how Indian fi­nance was built: 25 years in which the fi­nance min­istry, SEBI, NSE and aca­demics worked to­gether, and how re­form pe­tered out once that group scat­tered.

laughs.text: Amit’s self-diagnosis riff­ing on ‘Rebel Without a Cause’: as a teenager he was a rebel with­out a cause, ‘or if we wish to al­lit­er­ate, a rebel with­out restraints’, and today he is ‘a rebel with rules.’
A sly dig at dy­nas­ties: ‘we in­stinc­tively pre­fer strong men, or even strong women some­times, es­pe­cially if they’re from a fam­ily of an ear­lier strong man.’
Ajay de­scrib­ing the pol­i­cy­maker who wants to squeeze trapped for­eign firms: ‘the clever pol­icy maker, okay, it’s Indian IAS level of IQ.’
Amit to lis­ten­ers: ‘Ajay Shah reads pa­pers the way other ado­les­cent boys watch porn.’ You start one paper at 9 PM and sud­denly it’s 4 AM and you’ve gone through forty.

Ajay’s car­i­ca­ture of how many econ­o­mists think pol­icy hap­pens: they ‘whis­per in the ears of Aurangzeb and mirac­u­lously some pol­icy will happen’, until Aurangzeb ‘wakes up from the wrong side of the bed’ or some­one else whis­pers in his ear.

Amit makes Ajay roll up his sleeve and flex for the cam­era (‘Nomsita, can we zoom, please?’), then points out that the bi­ceps came from a rules-based regime, not from doing what­ever ex­er­cise he felt like.

Ajay pitches row­ing to any­one who is ‘a lazy bum’ or ‘a sleepy Bengali’. Amit hits back with a Hindi pun: his Bengali melo­drama makes him want to weep co­pi­ously and be­come a ‘rona’ (cry­ing) ma­chine. He adds that Bengal gave India Rabindra Sangeet and Satyajit Ray, while Gujarat gave ‘a diet that is guar­an­teed to pro­duce di­a­betes. Well done.’

Amit on the final rec­om­men­da­tions: ‘I am rec­om­mend­ing a geeky schol­arly book and he is rec­om­mend­ing a row­ing ma­chine… This is a man of ac­tion. So I guess the sec­ond half of your life will be more ac­tion than thought.’

Mark Antony’s speech over Caesar’s corpse in Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar (‘You are not wood, you are not stones, but men’), which Ajay adapts into his per­sonal eco­nom­ics slo­gan: ‘…and being men, you will op­ti­mize.’

Ram Rajya and the mai-baap state: Ajay says we grow up imag­in­ing the strong­man will be a Ram, a ruler who grants wishes ‘straight out of Hindu mythology’, and that a good coun­try is one where he can grant very few.
Indira Gandhi’s 1970s top in­come tax rate of about 97% (Amit’s fig­ure), of­fered as proof that push­ing rates up doesn’t bring in pro­por­tion­ally more and didn’t make India a boom­ing econ­omy.
‘Tryst with Destiny’ as the first chap­ter of Salman Rushdie’s an­thol­ogy of Indian writ­ing, used as ev­i­dence that great lead­ers pair thought with elo­quent ar­tic­u­la­tion.

From an ear­lier de­cen­tral­i­sa­tion dis­cus­sion: Japan has about thirty va­ri­eties of Kit Kat, while India has ‘only one Maggi, one Kit Kat’. Amit uses it to show how uni­form rules can ig­nore local tastes.
